summary:
The DETECT Fentanyl and Xylazine Act of 2024, Pub. L. 118-186, amends the Homeland Security Act of 2002 to add to the responsibilities of the Department of Homeland Security Science and Technology Directorate a new research, development, testing, evaluation, and cost-benefit analysis function directed at improving drug detection equipment and reference libraries.

Section 2 amends section 302 of the Homeland Security Act of 2002, 6 U.S.C. § 182, by adding new paragraph (15). The new paragraph directs the Directorate, in coordination with the Drug Enforcement Administration, to carry out research, development, testing, evaluation, and cost-benefit analyses to improve the safety, effectiveness, and efficiency of equipment, and the effectiveness and efficiency of reference libraries, for use by Federal, State, local, Tribal, and territorial law enforcement agencies in accurately detecting drugs, including fentanyl and xylazine. The covered technologies include: portable equipment capable of detecting and identifying drugs with minimal or no sample handling; equipment capable of separating complex mixtures containing low concentrations of drugs and high concentrations of cutting agents into component parts to enable signature extraction for field identification and detection; and technologies using machine learning or “artificial intelligence,” as defined in section 5002 of the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020, 15 U.S.C. § 9401, and other techniques to predict whether substances in a sample are controlled substance analogues or other new psychoactive substances not yet included in available reference libraries.

Section 3, codified as a note to 6 U.S.C. § 182, imposes implementation requirements on the Under Secretary for Science and Technology in carrying out new section 302(15). The Under Secretary must follow the recommendations, guidelines, and best practices in the Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (NIST AI 100-1), or any successor document issued by the National Institute of Standards and Technology. The Under Secretary also must establish research, development, testing, evaluation, and cost-benefit analysis priorities under section 302(15) based on the latest available information, including specific drugs identified as threats in DHS’s latest Homeland Threat Assessment, DEA’s latest State and Territory Report on Enduring and Emerging Threats, or successor documents.

Section 4, also codified as a note to 6 U.S.C. § 182, provides that the Act may not be construed to limit the authority of agencies currently managing, overseeing, or otherwise involved in drug equipment and reference libraries. The Act contains no authorization of appropriations, direct appropriation, sunset, or delayed effective date.
